item.title: [Critical] Bloomberg: hackers reached tanker VL Prosperity’s propulsion system — the FBI reports no disruption and no attacker is named
item.category: Top Story
item.description: On 2 October Bloomberg, citing unnamed US officials, reported that FBI and Coast Guard investigators found hackers had accessed the propulsion system of the crude supertanker VL Prosperity as it neared the Texas coast this summer. Neither agency has confirmed that on the record, and how long the access lasted, or what it could control, is unknown. The FBI says it has no reports of operational disruption, vessel instability, danger to crews or environmental harm. The confirmed part dates from September: cyber teams boarded two foreign-flagged, US-bound energy tankers in August after signs their networks were compromised, which the Coast Guard attributes to foreign cyber actors. Per Dragos, VL Prosperity was boarded on 21 August in the Atlantic and the second, unnamed tanker on 24 August. As of 23 October no new official statement had been found, and the latest coverage dates from 5 October. For terminal operators, the exposure is the ship-shore interface. - Bloomberg report of 2 Oct 2026, as syndicated by gCaptain and SupplyChainBrain, citing unnamed US officials, with the FBI’s on-record statement; joint US Coast Guard and FBI statement via CyberScoop and The Record; Rear Adm. Grable via CBS News; boarding dates and VL Prosperity’s boarding location per Dragos (“VL Prosperity: What MTSA Cybersecurity Already Requires”, 24 Sep 2026); engine-room claims trace to Iranian state media and are unverified; the second vessel has not been named by the agencies - Boardings 21 and 24 Aug 2026; publicly confirmed 16 Sep 2026; Dragos commentary 24 Sep 2026; Bloomberg propulsion-system report 2 Oct 2026, not confirmed on the record; latest coverage found 5 Oct 2026; no new official statement found to 23 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Microsoft ties the ConnectWise cloud compromise to China-aligned Storm-0940, which used the vendor’s own app identities to reach Microsoft 365 tenants — energy and chemicals are on its target list
item.category: Incident — Supply-chain compromise of a managed-service cloud app; China-state aligned actor per Microsoft; energy and chemicals among targeted sectors; no OT impact reported
item.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence wrote on 21 October that it assesses Storm-0940, an actor it calls China-state aligned, was responsible for the recently disclosed compromise of ConnectWise’s cloud services. The attacker gained control of the identities of several ConnectWise cloud applications, ConnectWise Cloud Backup among them, and used their stolen credentials to sign in to customers’ Microsoft 365 tenants as the trusted app, so the users’ multi-factor authentication never came into play. Microsoft says Storm-0940 drove the campaign with ARTEX, an open-source penetration-testing framework that can use any AI model, and attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants; most of the targeting failed, but it gained privileged cloud persistence at many organisations within a short time. A separate password spray from 10 to 14 October produced no successful sign-in. Once inside, it ran directory reconnaissance, added credentials to applications and changed roles and groups. ConnectWise shut down Cloud Backup, took its SaaS Security and Cloud Management services offline and disabled the affected app identities, and says it has seen no indication so far that partner backup data was compromised. Microsoft lists aerospace and defence, chemicals, energy, manufacturing and government among the targeted sectors; it names no victims, and no OT impact has been reported. The sector read is ours: a Microsoft 365 tenant holds the email, SharePoint libraries and Teams channels where plant drawings, network diagrams, vendor remote-access details and incident plans tend to live, and many operators and their contractors buy backup through managed service providers. - Microsoft Threat Intelligence blog (21 Oct 2026, updated 23 Oct); ConnectWise service actions as reported by BleepingComputer; other published tenant counts conflict and are not given here; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - ConnectWise services suspended mid-October 2026; Microsoft attribution published 21 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] FBI and Secret Service: the FortiBleed credential campaign against FortiGate firewalls is still running — and the energy sector is among its targets
item.category: Active campaign — FBI and Secret Service warning on FortiGate credential theft; energy among targeted sectors; no CVE; no OT compromise described
item.description: In a joint advisory dated Tuesday 6 October (JCSA-20261006-01), the FBI and US Secret Service warned that the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways remains an active threat, with attackers still scanning for devices they can log into using credentials obtained earlier. There is no CVE: the agencies describe abuse of reused or leaked credentials and of legacy SHA-256 password storage. Researcher reporting adds credential stuffing and spraying from leak dumps, offline cracking of extracted hashes and a tool, FortigateSniffer, that passively captures authentication traffic across 24 protocols. Intruders have created administrator accounts with names such as fortiAdmin, forticloud-sync and fgtsecure, and some owners were locked out after attackers reset or deleted the legitimate accounts. The agencies say targets span all 16 US critical infrastructure sectors, energy and food and agriculture among them, and the FBI links the access to Payload ransomware; SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments that began this way. SOCRadar’s figure of 86,644 working device credentials in 194 countries dates from 19 June and is not a new count. Researchers describe the operator as a Russian-speaking initial access broker whose buyers overlap with INC and Lynx affiliates; that is their assessment, not the agencies’. No OT system compromise has been described and no oil and gas victim named. The sector read is ours: FortiGate is one of the most common firewalls at the IT/OT boundary and at remote sites, so a working login on one is a step toward operations. - FBI and US Secret Service joint advisory JCSA-20261006-01 (6 Oct 2026), as reported by Cybersecurity Dive and The Hacker News (7 Oct 2026); ransomware counts, credential figures and the operator profile are SOCRadar and researcher assessments; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Campaign first documented June 2026; agency warning 6 Oct 2026; reported 7 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] CenterPoint Energy tells Texas its customer-data breach reached 1,062,060 residents — and still says gas and electric operations were not affected
item.category: Incident — Customer data breach at a gas and electric utility, now more than 1 million Texans; no operational impact
item.description: CenterPoint Energy, the Houston-based electric and natural gas utility, has told the Texas Attorney General’s Office that 1,062,060 Texas residents were affected by the breach it disclosed in September, SecurityWeek reported on 15 October. As SecurityWeek describes the filing, the exposed data includes names, addresses, Social Security numbers and driver’s licence numbers; residents of Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio may also be affected, and no overall total has been given. The company again says the incident did not affect its operations. In its SEC filing CenterPoint said an unauthorised party obtained customer information through one of its external-facing systems and that it learned of the breach from the actor’s own public post; BleepingComputer reported in September that the system was a public API with no rate limiting, web application firewall or automated access controls. The actor claimed nearly 7.5 million records and posted a 2.5 GB archive on 12 September; the company has not confirmed that figure, and class-action filings allege the intrusion ran from 17 August to 1 September. This is an IT and customer-data incident, not an OT one, and it is scored that way. It belongs on an oil and gas page because gas distribution utilities run customer-facing APIs alongside SCADA for pressure and flow, and the useful question is how much those two estates share. - CenterPoint Energy filing with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, as reported by SecurityWeek (15 Oct 2026); SEC filing and API detail as reported by BleepingComputer and The Record in September; record count claimed by the actor, not confirmed by the company - Intrusion alleged 17 Aug–1 Sep 2026; company disclosure 15 Sep 2026; Texas filing reported 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] The FBI seizes domains behind Microscan and FishHub, China-linked tools whose targets included gas and power companies — no OT intrusion is described
item.category: Threat Intelligence — US seizure of China-linked scanning and phishing tooling; gas and power companies among named targets; no compromise of those targets confirmed
item.description: On 8 October the Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorised seizures, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, of domains used to run two tools: Microscan, a Python web application with more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts, supported by a Mirai-variant IoT botnet, and FishHub, used for spear-phishing and malware delivery. US authorities tie the tooling to China-based Integrity Technology Group, the company sanctioned last year and linked to a 2024 botnet takedown. The attribution wording varies: CyberScoop calls the tools Flax Typhoon-linked, while Cybersecurity Dive says the company’s activity mimics that of the group tracked as Flax Typhoon rather than equating the two. Court documents, as Cybersecurity Dive reports them, list Microscan targets including a South Carolina power company, airports in Japan and Poland, a multinational NGO, and gas and power companies in Taiwan; FishHub was aimed at Taiwanese universities. None of those targets has been confirmed as compromised. A joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory accompanied the seizures, and CISA’s Chris Butera said China-affiliated actors continue to position themselves inside critical infrastructure networks, OT systems included. No operational impact is described. For oil and gas the link is direct rather than inferred: gas companies were on the target list of a state-linked scanning platform, and scanning is the stage that comes before access. - DOJ and FBI announcement and joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory, as reported by CyberScoop (8 Oct 2026) and Cybersecurity Dive (9 Oct 2026); target list from court documents as reported; attribution wording differs between outlets; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Seizures announced 8 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] Insurer Resilience: ransomware was 9% of its energy and utility claims but about 70% of the losses — and none of the claims involved control-system manipulation
item.category: Research — Insurer claims data for energy and utilities; no control-system manipulation in any claim
item.description: Cyber insurer Resilience has published an analysis of the energy and utilities claims it received between January 2023 and early September 2026, reported by Industrial Cyber on 21 October. Ransomware made up about 9% of the sector’s claims, against 6% elsewhere in Resilience’s book, but drove about 70% of incurred losses. Email compromise was more common, at 21% of energy claims compared with 10% elsewhere, yet accounted for only 2% of losses; malware was 7% of claims. About 17% of energy claims began at a vendor, and roughly a third of those vendors were HR, payroll, benefits or accounting firms. Attackers got past multi-factor authentication by talking people out of one-time codes and by hijacking sessions, and clients with tested backups and segmentation recovered or kept production running. None of the energy claims, water and wastewater clients included, involved control-system manipulation; Resilience says claims data probably understates OT risk, because OT intrusions can go unnoticed. This is one insurer’s portfolio, not a census of the sector. The read for oil and gas is ours: the losses that land are business-side ransomware and the shutdowns it forces, so recovering the systems that schedule, measure and bill product matters as much as protecting the control network. - Resilience report “Cyber risk in energy and utilities: Lessons from Insurance Claims” as reported by Industrial Cyber (21 Oct 2026); claims period 1 Jan 2023 to 5 Sep 2026; oil and gas application is editorial assessment - Reported 21 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] Securing the remote wellsite: an Industrial Cyber feature collects Dragos’s finding that oil and gas has the weakest IT/OT segmentation of any sector, and practitioners’ advice on vendor access
item.category: Research — Industry feature on securing upstream oil and gas; data from earlier in 2026; no new incident
item.description: Industrial Cyber published a feature on 20 October on securing upstream oil and gas operations across distance, remoteness and harsh environments. It reports no new incident or advisory, and its data come from earlier in 2026. It cites Dragos’s 2026 OT/ICS year in review: poor IT/OT segmentation appeared in 29% of Dragos’s oil and gas cases, the highest share of any sector, and the group Dragos tracks as VOLTZITE compromised cellular gateways across US oil and gas infrastructure before moving into engineering workstations. A Tosi survey of 100 US upstream and midstream OT leaders found 87% confident they could detect a breach within 24 hours, but only 16% credited continuous OT monitoring for that confidence. The practitioners quoted converge on remote access. Dragos’s Michael Hoffman points to legacy RTUs and radio networks built for reliability rather than authentication, and recommends MFA, brokered jump hosts and recorded, time-bound sessions. OMV Petrom’s Albert Vartic would limit remote control to predefined safe actions, keep shutdowns local and keep safety systems independent of networked control. Thales’s Edwin Loke warns of vendor “shadow access”, such as unmanaged 4G routers, at unattended sites. - Industrial Cyber feature by Anna Ribeiro (20 Oct 2026), citing Dragos’s 2026 OT/ICS year in review and a Tosi survey; the statistics are secondary and predate this edition’s window - Published 20 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Attackers forced defrost on refrigeration controllers in about 700 French supermarkets — a food-sector attack, and a test for every vendor-managed controller you expose
item.category: Cross-sector lesson — confirmed OT attack on supermarket refrigeration controllers in France; not an oil and gas incident; sector link is editorial assessment
item.description: Over the nights of 11–13 October, the second wave hitting stores with Dixell equipment, attackers remotely changed settings on web-managed refrigeration controllers in French supermarkets, forcing extended defrost cycles that pushed cabinets toward about 50°C and spoiled stock; the Paris prosecutor reports fires at some sites. Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on 13 October that roughly 700 of France’s 10,000 supermarkets were hit, across Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché and Netto, and Monoprix. CERT-FR’s alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 named Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers on 12 October, added Copeland and Dixell xweb on 13 October, and on 16 October said the campaigns are probably still under way; as of 23 October CERT-FR had issued no later version, and no new attack nights had been reported since 13 October. No actor has claimed it, no ransom has been demanded and the entry route has not been established; Danfoss and Copeland say most affected units are older, end-of-life models. Two follow-ups reach beyond retail. Nozomi Networks’ 13 October analysis links the same precondition — controllers left reachable from the internet for vendor management — to fuel automatic tank gauges, citing Shadowserver’s count of 909 exposed gauges in June. And Claroty Team82 reported on 13 October that an AI coding agent, redirected by a human, reproduced a previously disclosed Danfoss AK-SM 800A authentication-bypass and command-injection chain to root on a lab device in about 28 minutes for roughly $6; Team82 does not say those flaws were used in France. On 22 October Forescout counted 12,976 internet-exposed refrigeration management service observations on 6,017 IP addresses in 99 countries — services, not devices. This is not an oil and gas incident and it does not count toward this page’s score. The lesson is ours: tank gauges, forecourt and convenience-store refrigeration, building management and vendor-monitored packages at terminals and retail fuel sites belong to the same exposure class. - CERT-FR alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 (v1 12 Oct, v2 13 Oct, v3 16 Oct 2026); Finance Minister Lescure via AP (13 Oct 2026); affected chains per SecurityWeek (15 Oct 2026); Nozomi Networks analysis and Claroty Team82 research (13 Oct 2026); Forescout Vedere Labs exposure count (22 Oct 2026); exposure counts are third-party figures; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Attacks on the nights of 11–13 Oct 2026; CERT-FR alert updated 16 Oct 2026, no later version as of 23 Oct; Forescout count 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] Dragos: old worms such as Conficker, Sality and WannaCry keep turning up in OT incident calls — and the wrong cleanup can do more harm than the infection
item.category: Research — Commodity malware in OT networks and how to clean it up; vendor guidance, no actor
item.description: Dragos’s Lesley Carhart and Jan Hoff wrote on 15 October that requests for help with legacy commodity infections — Sality, Gammima, WannaCry and Conficker among them — have risen sharply in recent years. Many OT networks Dragos is called into carry between 20 and 70 distinct commodity-malware variants spread across several subnets, often on systems older than Windows XP SP2. They put the rise down to more networking and remote access, better visibility, and regulation that expects critical-infrastructure networks to be clean. Their answer is a triage framework they call Now, Next and Never, published with a white paper, and a warning that a cleanup done the wrong way can be riskier than the infection it is meant to remove. There is no CVE and no actor here. The fit for oil and gas is our assessment and an easy one: refineries, gas plants and pipeline control centres keep operator stations, historians and vendor PCs on old Windows builds for years, and an aggressive cleanup — mass reboots, forced updates or an endpoint agent pushed onto running units — can stop a process the worm never touched. - Dragos blog by Lesley Carhart and Jan Hoff (15 Oct 2026), with its linked white paper; oil and gas application is editorial assessment - Published 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Symantec: the China-nexus group behind Warlock ransomware broke into a water utility and a telecom operator through on-premises SharePoint — no OT impact is described, and no energy victim is named
item.category: Threat Intelligence — China-nexus ransomware intrusions via SharePoint; water and telecom victims; cross-sector context, no OT impact described
item.description: Symantec’s Threat Hunter Team reported on 1 October that a group it calls Longlegs, which it describes as a China-nexus threat actor also tracked as Storm-2603, has attacked at least four organisations in the past two months: two critical infrastructure operators — a water utility and a telecommunications provider — plus a regional government body and a university, in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries in Europe, Africa and Latin America. No victim or country is named. Symantec says the group typically gets in by exploiting several vulnerabilities in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server; the CVEs it names are the 2025 ToolShell flaws (CVE-2025-49704, CVE-2025-49706, CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771), alongside unspecified related SharePoint flaws. Once inside, the group steals ASP.NET machine keys, sideloads DLLs, uses Visual Studio Code tunnels and NetExec, and loads a vulnerable signed driver (CVE-2025-1055 in K7RKScan) to switch off security tools; in one intrusion Symantec documents, Warlock was pushed to at least 33 hosts through SYSVOL. Symantec does not describe any operational or OT impact at the water utility and does not say ransomware was deployed there. It is on this page as cross-sector context, not an oil and gas incident: the targets are critical infrastructure operators, the entry point is the kind of on-premises collaboration server that engineering and document-control teams often run, and machine-key theft means a server patched after compromise can still be reopened. - Symantec Threat Hunter Team report, with coverage by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek; attribution and victim descriptions are Symantec’s; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Published 1 Oct 2026; intrusions over the preceding two months

item.title: [Medium] Recorded Future: Russia’s hybrid pressure on Europe is “largely opportunistic” for now — and a drone intercepted near Romania’s Neptun Deep offshore gas field is among its cases
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Nation-state hybrid threat assessment; physical and cyber; no new OT impact
item.description: Recorded Future’s Insikt Group published an assessment on 24 September that Russia has escalated what it calls “New Generation Warfare” tactics in Europe since February 2022, combining sabotage, drones, cyber operations and disinformation. It judges current activity “largely opportunistic”, but likely to escalate over the next two years, potentially culminating in a full-scale campaign. The incidents it cites include an explosive maritime drone intercepted near Romania’s Neptun Deep offshore gas field on 20 August 2026, a sabotage plot using military-grade explosives against cargo infrastructure at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August, DDoS and access operations against the Norwegian public sector on 30 August, and subsea cables as a growing target. Dark Reading’s coverage adds that the research cites water and wastewater targeting in Norway and Poland and attacks on Poland’s energy infrastructure in early 2026. Insikt’s recommendations include contractor and insider vetting, perimeter detection and anti-drone measures, alternative supply routes, coordination with national CERTs and phishing-resistant MFA. This is an analytic assessment attributed to Russia at assessment level; the blog names no specific unit and reports no new OT process impact. It is separate from the ENISA threat landscape below. For operators with European offshore, pipeline and terminal assets the relevance is direct: the physical and cyber threats are being assessed together, so the security planning for those assets should be too. - Recorded Future Insikt Group blog (24 Sep 2026), with additional detail as reported by Dark Reading; attribution is Insikt’s assessment; oil and gas application is editorial assessment - Published 24 Sep 2026; Neptun Deep drone intercept 20 Aug 2026

item.title: [Medium] Microsoft profiles Storm-2570, a ransomware affiliate that switches between Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis and BERT while its tradecraft stays the same — energy and chemicals are on its victim list
item.category: Threat Intelligence — Ransomware affiliate tradecraft; energy and chemicals among victim sectors; IT-side, no OT impact reported
item.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence published a profile on 24 September of Storm-2570, a ransomware affiliate it has tracked since April 2025 that has deployed Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis and BERT ransomware. Microsoft lists victims in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Spain, the Netherlands and Puerto Rico, in sectors that include energy, chemicals, critical manufacturing and transportation as well as healthcare, education, government and financial services. It says the method of initial access “remains unconfirmed”. The tooling is mostly legitimate software: remote-management agents including Atera, MeshAgent, ScreenConnect, Splashtop and NinjaRMM; PsExec, Impacket and NetExec for lateral movement; Mimikatz, LaZagne and ntdsutil for credentials; ngrok and Cloudflare tunnels; and Rclone and s5cmd for exfiltration. Microsoft names no individual victim and describes no OT impact. Two points carry over to oil and gas. Switching ransomware brands changes the leak site, not the behaviour, so detections built on behaviour — a new RMM agent, PsExec from an unusual host, an ntdsutil run — keep working when the brand changes. And the same RMM tools are common in vendor support for plant, pipeline and terminal systems, which makes an allow-list of approved remote tools an OT control as well as an IT one. - Microsoft Threat Intelligence blog (24 Sep 2026), reviewed directly; no victims named; oil and gas application is editorial assessment - Published 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] NCC Group counts 1,073 ransomware attacks in August, a 2026 high, with the industrial sector bearing 31% — and energy incidents are still landing on IT, which is where the outage comes from
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Ransomware statistics
item.description: NCC Group’s review of August 2026, reported by Industrial Cyber on 28 September, counts 1,073 ransomware attacks, up 12 percent from 960 in July. The industrial sector accounted for 329 of them, about 31 percent, and North America for 473, about 44 percent. Qilin led with 164 claimed attacks, overtaking The Gentlemen. NCC also describes Aurora, a ransomware-as-a-service group active since late April that goes after manufacturing, legal, research and transportation organisations through weak or unauthenticated VPN access before encrypting hypervisors. A different tracker, Comparitech, reported on 14 September a record 997 attacks for the same month; the counts differ because each tracker has its own method, and both rest largely on leak-site claims, so a claimed victim is not a confirmed one, and neither breaks out oil and gas. The pattern they fit is the one the sector already knows from Colonial Pipeline onward — encryption lands on business systems, and operations stop because scheduling, billing, custody-transfer accounting or terminal ticketing depends on them, not because anything touched a controller. - NCC Group’s monthly ransomware review, reported by Industrial Cyber; Comparitech tracking, reported by Industrial Cyber; both counts rest largely on actor claims and do not break out oil and gas - Data for August 2026; Comparitech figures reported 14 Sep 2026; NCC Group figures reported 28 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Ivanti Connect Secure: a three-flaw chain gave attackers root on fully patched VPNs — two flaws fixed under CVE-2026-104935, in KEV due 16 October; the third has no patch
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited VPN zero-day chain, CISA KEV; one link still unpatched
item.description: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that a limited number of Connect Secure customers had been attacked through a chain of three flaws that gives an unauthenticated attacker root on a fully patched appliance. Two of them — an authentication bypass by spoofing and a file write that together allow unauthenticated command execution — are fixed under a single CVE, CVE-2026-104935, which Ivanti scores CVSS v3.1 8.6; the fixed releases are 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1. The third, a privilege-escalation bug in an internal broker service, has no CVE and no patch yet; Ivanti expects a fix in the coming weeks, and we found no public report of one as of 23 October. Volexity found the chain during an incident response and tracks the actor as UTA0576, a new name. Its case began on 3 October on a fully patched appliance, and Defused saw activity from 1 October, so exploitation dates from at least early October. The intruders left no web shell or backdoor. They ran commands through the exploit itself, took domain credentials stored on the appliance, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, Kerberoasted, sprayed passwords, sniffed LDAP traffic and wiped logs. Volexity and CISA warn that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect this compromise because the chain alters code in memory, so a clean result is not proof. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 13 October with a 16 October deadline. Volexity has only low confidence that the motive is criminal rather than espionage. No oil and gas victim has been named. The sector read is ours: Connect Secure is a common front door for engineers and vendors into OT DMZs, and this chain hands an outsider the domain credentials behind it. - Ivanti advisory for CVE-2026-104935 and Volexity research (13 Oct 2026), as reported by SecurityWeek, CyberScoop and Cybersecurity Dive; Defused observations via Cybersecurity Dive; CISA KEV entry; OT remote-access relevance is editorial assessment - Exploitation from at least early October 2026; disclosed and added to KEV 13 Oct 2026; federal deadline 16 Oct 2026; no public fix for the third flaw found as of 23 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, exploited since late August by a suspected China-nexus espionage group, is now in KEV — CISA set a 19 October deadline for federal agencies
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-support appliance zero-day exploited by a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor; in CISA KEV since 16 Oct
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-102764, a flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support, to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October federal deadline, a day after Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reported that it had been exploited as a zero-day from late August. GTIG attributes the activity to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221, on the strength of tooling and technique overlap. The flaw is improper validation of message origins in Remote Support’s internal messaging, which lets an attacker carry out file operations on the appliance; BeyondTrust scores it CVSS v4.0 9.3, and every Remote Support release up to 26.2.3 is affected. SecurityWeek reports that two appliances were compromised, one hosted by BeyondTrust and one self-hosted. The intruders gained root, installed a PHP web shell GTIG calls SAWFLY and a SOCKS5 tunneller it calls BARECLAW, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the product’s own file-transfer feature to pull documents from user desktops. BeyondTrust identified the defect on 28 September, shipped patch BT26-05-RS on 8 October for releases 24.3.1 to 26.2.3, and had patched all SaaS customers by 9 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand, and releases older than 24.3.1 must upgrade first. GTIG names no victims or sectors and advises treating any internet-reachable appliance that ran a vulnerable release during the window as potentially compromised. The sector read is ours: remote-support tools are how many IT help desks, OEMs and integrators reach operator stations and engineering PCs, so a compromised support appliance is a ready-made path to the plant side. - Google Threat Intelligence Group blog (15 Oct 2026); BeyondTrust advisory BT26-05; CISA KEV entry (added 16 Oct 2026); compromise and timeline details as reported by SecurityWeek and The Record (16 Oct 2026); CVSS from the CVE record; OT relevance is editorial assessment - Exploited from late August 2026; defect identified 28 Sep; fix shipped 8 Oct, SaaS patched 9 Oct; disclosed 15 Oct; added to KEV 16 Oct 2026 (due 19 Oct)

item.title: [Critical] Citrix NetScaler: a fourth critical flaw (CVSS 9.5) follows three exploited ones — and builds that fixed the zero-days stay exposed when used as a SAML identity provider
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access gateway; three exploited flaws in CISA KEV and a fourth critical flaw patched 8 Oct
item.description: On 8 October Citrix published bulletin CTX697191 for CVE-2026-107406, a memory overflow in NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider, which Citrix says may lead to remote code execution or denial of service. It is scored CVSS v4.0 9.5, has no workaround, and Citrix says it is not aware of exploitation; it was still not in KEV as of CISA’s 21 October catalog. The catch is that builds which fixed the late-September zero-days — 14.1-73.37 to 73.41 and 13.1-64.23 to 64.28 — remain vulnerable when the appliance acts as a SAML identity provider, and older builds are vulnerable in either role, so many sites must upgrade again, to 14.1-73.46 or 13.1-64.29 and later (13.1-37.283 for FIPS and NDcPP). The three earlier flaws are confirmed exploited and in KEV. CVE-2026-88771, unauthenticated command execution, and CVE-2026-88772, a memory overflow that needs DTLS (on by default on VPN virtual servers), both CVSS v4 9.5, were patched and listed on 27 September. CVE-2026-88779, a SAML memory overflow scored 8.7, was patched on 3 October and listed on 4 October; Citrix and watchTowr describe it as a crash bug, and CISA has warned it is used to force reboots so that code planted through 88771 runs. CISA has renewed its call to patch and released Sigma detection rules. Google Threat Intelligence and LevelBlue describe what intruders leave behind: a PHP web shell (WHIPSHOT), a Python tunneller (SLAPSHOT), a rogue superuser account named sec_monitor and stolen configuration archives. Mandiant describes dozens of victim organisations across North America and Europe and suspected state-nexus actors, unnamed; Arctic Wolf counts at least 78 targeted organisations, which is not a count of confirmed compromises; Shadowserver sees more than 20,000 exposed or potentially vulnerable appliances. Upgrading does not remove an intruder who is already in. No oil and gas victim has been named. The sector read is ours: NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for vendor and engineer remote access into refinery, gas-plant and pipeline OT DMZs. - Citrix bulletins CTX697096, CTX697174 and CTX697191; CISA KEV entries and alerts; CVE-2026-107406 record and fixed builds via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup and The Hacker News (9 Oct 2026); CISA’s renewed warning via Cybersecurity Dive (12 Oct 2026); post-exploitation findings from Google Threat Intelligence and LevelBlue; victim and exposure counts from Mandiant, Arctic Wolf and Shadowserver; OT remote-access relevance is editorial assessment - Two zero-days patched and added to KEV 27 Sep 2026; third flaw patched 3 Oct, added to KEV 4 Oct; fourth flaw disclosed 8 Oct 2026; CISA renewed its patch call, reported 12 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] KEV, 13–15 October: an exploited PAN-OS root flaw, a CVSS 9.8 Cisco email-gateway bug and the Windows zero-day from Patch Tuesday, all on three-day deadlines
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA KEV additions 13–15 Oct: boundary firewall, mail gateway and Windows zero-days
item.description: CISA added seven CVEs to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog between 13 and 15 October; Ivanti’s has its own card. The one closest to OT is CVE-2026-0322 in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS, added on 14 October: an attacker with credentials and network access to the management interface of a PA-Series or VM-Series firewall or Panorama can run code as root. Palo Alto, which found it internally, reports very limited exploitation, scores it CVSS v4.0 8.6 and lists fixed releases including 12.2.4, 12.1.10-h2, 11.2.16, 11.1.16-h3 and 10.2.18-h12; Prisma Access and Cloud NGFW are not affected. Also on 14 October came CVE-2026-76519 in Cisco Secure Email Gateway, CVSS 9.8: a sender with no login can write files and reach root through a crafted attachment where File Reputation is enabled on a mail policy and Content Scanner Tools are older than 25.3.0.5525. Cisco is aware of attacks this month; the fixes are AsyncOS 15.5.5-014 or 16.5.0-780 (the 16.0 train must migrate) or the Content Scanner Tools update. It is separate from CVE-2026-76461, a SQL-injection flaw in the same gateway that was exploited and added to KEV in September. On 13 October CISA listed CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell security-feature bypass (CVSS 8.8) that Microsoft’s October update fixed among more than 1,400 CVEs; SecurityWeek describes it as a Mark-of-the-Web bypass that needs a user to open a file. The rest were AhsayCBS backup-server flaws CVE-2026-105133 and -105134 (14 October) and Atlassian Data Center CVE-2026-21589 (15 October). Deadlines run from 16 to 18 October. No victims or actors are named for any of them. The sector read is ours: PAN-OS firewalls commonly sit at refinery and pipeline IT/OT boundaries, and Windows engineering workstations and HMIs are where a mail-borne file ends up. - CISA KEV catalog (version 2026.10.15); Palo Alto Networks advisory for CVE-2026-0322; Cisco advisory cisco-sa-esa-afw-zqYJkjxp as reported by The Hacker News and SecurityWeek; Microsoft’s October 2026 release as reported by SecurityWeek; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - KEV additions 13, 14 and 15 Oct 2026; deadlines 16–18 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] A Siemens Software Center flaw is being abused in a ClickFix malware campaign — CISA added it to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November deadline
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens’ software download and licensing app, abused in a ClickFix campaign; CISA KEV
item.description: Siemens Software Center, the Windows application that downloads, installs, activates and updates purchased Siemens software, loads DLLs from an uncontrolled search path. Tracked as CVE-2026-110936, the flaw lets an attacker who can place a crafted DLL where the program looks run code with its privileges; Siemens scores it CVSS v3.1 6.7 and v4.0 8.4. Siemens published advisory SSA-580366 on 15 October, added the fix on 17 October and on 19 October confirmed active exploitation: attackers are pairing a genuine, validly signed copy of the program (version 3.5.8.7) with their own DLLs, delivered in installer packages, as part of what Siemens calls the “Romulus” multi-platform ClickFix campaign, which tricks users into running commands themselves. Siemens says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached, names no final malware, and has published indicators and behavioural detections. Version 4.0.9.8 fixes the flaw, and existing installations update on their next start. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November deadline and republished the advisory as ICSA-26-295-03 on 22 October, listing energy among the affected sectors. Huntress reported the flaw. The sector read is ours: because the lure brings its own signed copy, patching installed copies does not by itself stop it, and application allow-listing that trusts anything Siemens-signed on engineering laptops and plant-office PCs may let it run. - Siemens ProductCERT advisory SSA-580366 (V1.0 15 Oct, V1.1 17 Oct, V1.2 19 Oct 2026) and Siemens ProductCERT post on active exploitation (19 Oct 2026); CISA KEV entry (20 Oct 2026) and ICSA-26-295-03 (22 Oct 2026); OT allow-listing relevance is editorial assessment - Advisory 15 Oct 2026; exploitation confirmed 19 Oct; added to KEV 20 Oct (due 3 Nov); CISA republication 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] The FortiOS flaw behind Unit 42’s Peerstitch case is in KEV — attackers inside a telecom MSP’s FortiManager reached root on managed FortiGates, and more than 500 firewall configurations were exposed
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited FortiOS privilege-escalation flaw used against a managed service provider’s FortiGates; CISA KEV
item.description: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reported on 14 October on an intrusion at a telecommunications managed service provider. The attackers got in through FortiManager CVE-2024-47575, the 2024 “FortiJump” flaw in the protocol FortiManager uses to manage FortiGates, then used CVE-2025-61624, a FortiOS command-line path traversal, to get root on managed firewalls, where they installed a loader Unit 42 calls PEERSTITCH and an SSH reverse-shell channel hidden in an Apache module. Configuration files, serial numbers and public addresses of more than 500 FortiGates the provider managed were taken; Unit 42 describes that as exposure of configuration and credential material, not confirmed intrusion into those customers’ networks. It tracks the activity as CL-STA-0954, which overlaps UNC5820, and names no state. CVE-2025-61624 was fixed in April 2026; Fortinet rates it Medium because it needs privileged, authenticated access, and now marks it known exploited. CISA added it to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October deadline. The CVE record also lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808, an industrial appliance that can run FortiOS, as affected. The sector read is ours: many pipeline, terminal and field networks have FortiGates managed by a carrier or MSP, and those firewalls’ configurations are a map of the OT boundary. - Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 report (14 Oct 2026); Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-122; CISA KEV entry (16 Oct 2026); RUGGEDCOM APE1808 per the CVE record; no numeric score is given because published figures differ; OT relevance is editorial assessment - Fix released April 2026; Unit 42 report 14 Oct 2026; added to KEV 16 Oct 2026 (due 19 Oct)

item.title: [High] Arista patches a third exploited VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day in four months — any logged-in tenant user can take operator control of the system that configures remote-site SD-WAN
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited SD-WAN orchestrator zero-day, the third in four months; not yet in KEV
item.description: Arista disclosed CVE-2026-114625 on 22 October, a SQL injection in the on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) that lets any authenticated user, down to the lowest built-in tenant role, gain operator privileges, act as a local superuser operator and affect the VCO host. The CVE record scores it CVSS v3.1 9.9 and v4.0 9.4. Arista says it detected the flaw itself, that it is known to be actively exploited and that no configuration prevents the exposure, and it has published two attacker addresses. The fixes are 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12; hosted and dedicated orchestrators have already been patched, and VeloCloud gateways and edges are not affected. It is the third exploited VCO zero-day since July, after CVE-2026-16812 (in KEV since 27 July) and September’s CVE-2026-93952 (in KEV since 22 September), so builds that fixed September’s flaw need upgrading again. It was not in KEV as of CISA’s 21 October catalog, which predates its publication. No victim or actor has been named. The sector read is ours: SD-WAN commonly links compressor and pump stations, terminals and field offices, and whoever holds the orchestrator can change routing, firewall and remote-access settings on every edge it manages. - Arista Security Advisory 0199 as reported by SecurityWeek, The Hacker News and BleepingComputer (22–23 Oct 2026); CVSS from the CVE record; earlier VCO flaws per CISA KEV; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Disclosed and patched 22 Oct 2026; not in KEV as of the 21 Oct 2026 catalog

item.title: [High] SonicWall SMA1000: a CVSS 10 pre-authentication flaw drew exploitation attempts two days after the fix — no confirmed breach, not in KEV
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access appliance, maximum-severity pre-authentication flaw; exploitation attempts reported; not in KEV
item.description: SonicWall published advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 on 6 October for CVE-2026-102255, a server-side request forgery in the Work Place interface of its SMA1000 remote-access appliances that it rates maximum severity; CISA’s enrichment scores it CVSS v3.1 10.0. Through an unintended alternate access path, an unauthenticated attacker can make the appliance send requests to its own internal functions. Affected are the SMA 6210, 7210 and 8200v on 12.4.3-03526 or older and 12.5.0-02952 or older; the fixes are 12.4.3-03670 and 12.5.0-03082, and there is no workaround. The same release fixes three flaws that need authentication: an OS command injection (CVE-2026-102256), a Zip Slip in the Appliance Management Console (CVE-2026-102257) and stored cross-site scripting (CVE-2026-102258). SMA 100 appliances and firewall SSL VPN are not affected. Defused saw its first hits on SMA decoys on 8 October and Previdian counted 135 attempts from two US addresses; reporting so far describes attempts, not successful break-ins, and the flaw was still not in KEV as of CISA’s 21 October catalog. SMA1000 has been a repeated target this year, including zero-days exploited in June. No oil and gas victim is named. The sector read is ours: SMA1000 appliances broker vendor and contractor access into industrial networks, and a pre-authentication flaw on that broker is a direct line toward the OT DMZ. - SonicWall advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 and the CVE record (CISA-ADP CVSS); exploitation attempts as reported by SecurityWeek, The Hacker News and Dark Reading (12 Oct 2026); OT remote-access relevance is editorial assessment - Fix published 6 Oct 2026; attempts observed from 8 Oct 2026; reported 12 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] PHP2Shell reaches OT software: Schneider Electric says EcoStruxure Control Engineering has no fix yet, and ABB and Moxa have issued notices — exploit attempts run into the millions, with no confirmed compromise
item.category: Critical Advisory — Critical PHP flaws under mass exploitation attempts reach OT engineering and process-automation software; one Schneider tool has no fix yet
item.description: Two PHP flaws known as PHP2Shell, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, let an unauthenticated attacker run code on servers that use PHP to answer web requests; the PHP security team rates each CVSS v4.0 9.2. Details leaked before the planned release, and PHP shipped fixes on 21 October in 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Amazon says exploitation attempts began on 17 October, four days before the patches; attempts have since run into the millions, but none of the reporting so far describes a confirmed successful compromise, and the CVEs were not in KEV as of CISA’s 21 October catalog. On 23 October PHP disclosed a further flaw, CVE-2026-115560, that applies only in an unusual session configuration and will be fixed in the next bugfix release. OT vendors have begun to respond. Schneider Electric’s bulletin SESB-2026-295-01 of 22 October lists EcoStruxure Security Expert, fixed in 1.48.4.0; ProLeiT LINEoptimize, with remediation through ProLeiT support; and EcoStruxure Control Engineering, for which Schneider has no fix yet and is establishing a remediation plan. The bulletin does not say how each product uses PHP or whether any has been attacked. ABB has listed a notice on APROL (SA26P015) and Moxa a response notice (MPSA-260001); neither document could be retrieved, so their details are not given here. The sector read is ours: process-automation engineering tools and their web components often sit on engineering networks that nobody scans as web servers. - Schneider Electric security notification SESB-2026-295-01 (22 Oct 2026); ABB and Moxa advisory listings (22–23 Oct 2026, documents not retrieved); PHP fixes and exploitation reporting via BleepingComputer and The Hacker News (21–23 Oct 2026), citing Amazon and other researchers; OT relevance is editorial assessment - Exploit attempts from 17 Oct 2026; PHP fixes 21 Oct; Schneider bulletin 22 Oct; follow-up PHP flaw disclosed 23 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Mitsubishi Electric fixes a CVSS v4.0 9.2 authentication bypass across ICONICS GENESIS64 and GENESIS — MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz will get no fix
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA/HMI and historian platform authentication bypass; three older products get no fix; not exploited
item.description: Mitsubishi Electric published advisory 2026-006 on 15 October for its ICONICS SCADA, HMI and historian software. The most serious flaw, CVE-2026-16436 (CVSS v4.0 9.2), is an authentication bypass: a fixed challenge-response mechanism lets a remote attacker who obtains the response unlock any user account. CVE-2026-16438 (v4.0 9.4) concerns default DCOM permissions granted to the administrator account; CVE-2026-16437 (v4.0 7.1) lets an administrator read and write the challenge-response file; and the libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 (v4.0 9.3) affects GENESIS64 and ICONICS Suite 10.97 to 10.97.2 where a local administrator imports a crafted file. Affected are GENESIS 11.03 and earlier; GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI and IoTWorX 10.97.3 and earlier; and all versions of MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz. The fixes are ICONICS Suite and IoTWorX 10.98, GENESIS 11.04 and, for libwebp, ICONICS Suite 10.97.3. Mitsubishi plans no fix for MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz and advises migration or its mitigations. It reports no exploitation, and none of the CVEs is in KEV. The sector read is ours: SCADA, HMI and historian platforms of this kind sit in control rooms and on terminal and plant networks, and older GENESIS32 and MC Works64 installations tend to run long after support ends. - Mitsubishi Electric PSIRT advisory 2026-006 (15 Oct 2026); CVSS v4.0 scores as published by Mitsubishi Electric; no CISA republication found in the 20 or 22 Oct batches; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Advisory published 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 20 October batch: a low-privileged user can get root on WAGO PFC and CC100 controllers, and Moxa’s AIG-302 edge gateway carries a hard-coded key — both fixed
item.category: Critical Advisory — CISA ICS advisories of 20 Oct: controller command injection to root and an edge-gateway hard-coded key; fixed; not exploited
item.description: CISA published five ICS advisories on 20 October, and two bear on field automation. ICSA-26-293-02 republishes WAGO’s CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-096 for devices on WAGO’s Linux-based firmware below 4.10.0 (FW32): the CC100, PFC100 G2 and PFC200 G2 controllers, TP600 panels, Edge Controller and WP400. CVE-2026-80466 (CVSS v3.1 8.8) is an OS command injection through routing parameters in the web-based management interface, which a low-privileged remote user can use to have a root-owned helper run commands; CVE-2026-88850 (v3.1 8.1) is a missing authorisation check that lets low-privileged users change root-owned PROFIBUS parameters. Firmware 4.10.0 (FW32) fixes both. ICSA-26-293-03 covers Moxa’s AIG-302 gateways running ThingsPro Edge firmware 1.4.0 and earlier: CVE-2026-109813, a hard-coded cryptographic key (v3.1 8.1, v4.0 8.6), and CVE-2026-109812, a missing authorisation check (v3.1 6.8, v4.0 6.9), both fixed in 1.4.1. CISA lists energy among the sectors for both, and no exploitation is reported. The batch’s other three advisories cover PEAK-System CAN drivers and revisions to two Hitachi Energy power-grid notices. The sector read is ours: compact controllers like these are common in packaged equipment and remote facilities, and edge gateways are how field data leaves a site. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-293-02 (WAGO, republishing CERT@VDE VDE-2026-096) and ICSA-26-293-03 (Moxa), read via CISA’s CSAF records on CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; Moxa advisory MPSA-262560; deployment context is editorial assessment - CISA advisories published 20 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Schneider Electric: Sage RTUs do not properly verify firmware authenticity — and Pro-face and Harmony STW6 HMIs carry an 8.8 flaw triggered from a web page
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA RTU firmware authenticity and HMI component flaws; Schneider Electric October notices; not exploited
item.description: Schneider Electric issued two new security notices on 13 October. SEVD-2026-286-02 covers its Sage remote terminal units — the 1410, 1430, 1450, 2400, 3030 Magnum and 4400 — which do not sufficiently verify that firmware is authentic. Under CVE-2026-102250, modified firmware can be loaded when an authorised administrator starts an update; Schneider scores it CVSS v3.1 7.2 (v4.0 8.6) with high privileges required, and the fix is firmware C3414-500-S02L0. SEVD-2026-286-01 covers Pro-face STW6000 and Harmony STW6 HMIs, all versions, where an unmaintained third-party component could let an attacker take control of the device if a user visits a malicious web page; CVE-2026-96434 scores CVSS v3.1 8.8 and needs that user interaction. Schneider also reissued an older Altivar drive notice (SEVD-2025-252-01, version 5.0) the same day. Neither new flaw is in KEV and no exploitation is reported. The sector read is ours, and this one sits close to the sector: Sage RTUs are a long-standing choice for pipeline, gas-measurement and utility telemetry, so the realistic attack is a tampered firmware file reaching a technician’s laptop before an update visit — which makes the provenance of firmware as important as the patch. - Schneider Electric security notices SEVD-2026-286-01 and SEVD-2026-286-02 (13 Oct 2026), with CVE records via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Published 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] October OT Patch Tuesday: S7-1500 web-server flaws at CVSS 9.6 with no fix yet, an Industrial Edge path traversal, and an ArmorBlock password takeover
item.category: Critical Advisory — October OT Patch Tuesday: Siemens S7-1500, Industrial Edge and CROSSBOW, Rockwell ArmorBlock; several fixes not yet available; not exploited
item.description: Siemens released its October advisories on 13 October; SecurityWeek counts 17. Three matter most for process plants. SSA-591731 covers eight web-server flaws (CVE-2026-63350 to -63357) in S7-1500, ET 200SP, ET 200pro and Drive Controller CPUs, all versions, that could let an attacker run code in an authorised user’s browser and carry out PLC operations with that user’s rights; Siemens scores the advisory CVSS v3.1 9.6 and has no fix yet, only mitigations. SSA-784472 lists 377 CVEs, up to CVSS 10.0, in the optional Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 TM MFP technology module — the module, not the CPUs — again with no fix yet. SSA-832641 is an authenticated path traversal in Industrial Edge devices and some HMI panels (CVE-2026-44415, CVSS 9.1), fixed for Edge devices, IoT2050 and IPCs but not yet for SCALANCE LPE9413/9433 or the affected panels. Siemens also fixed 11 flaws, up to CVSS 8.8, in RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW in version 6.0. Rockwell’s only new advisory, SD1801, covers 1732E ArmorBlock I/O modules on 3.012 and earlier: CVE-2026-12655 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) lets an unauthenticated attacker change the web-server password and take over the module, and CVE-2026-12656 (7.5) is a traffic-flood denial of service that needs a power cycle to clear; 3.013 fixes both and there is no workaround. Nothing in the set is in KEV or reported exploited. CISA republished the Siemens advisories on 22 October as ICSA-26-295-02 to -18, and the S7 web-server flaws and the S7-1500 MFP Linux-subsystem issues still had no fix. The sector read is ours: S7-1500 controllers and ArmorBlock I/O arrive inside compressor packages, terminal loading systems and vendor skids, which is where version tracking tends to fail. - Siemens ProductCERT advisories SSA-591731, SSA-784472, SSA-832641 and SSA-508506; Rockwell Automation advisory SD1801; advisory count per SecurityWeek’s 14 Oct 2026 roundup; CISA republications ICSA-26-295-02 to -18 (22 Oct 2026); oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Siemens and Rockwell advisories 13 Oct 2026; SecurityWeek roundup 14 Oct 2026; CISA republished the Siemens set 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA: an authorisation flaw in Inductive Automation Ignition lets users escalate their privileges — CVSS 8.8, fixed in 8.1.55 and 8.3.9
item.category: Critical Advisory — SCADA/HMI platform privilege escalation; CISA ICS advisory; not exploited
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-286-01 on 13 October for Inductive Automation’s Ignition SCADA and HMI platform. CVE-2026-92817 is an incorrect-authorisation flaw that allows privilege escalation, scored CVSS v3.1 8.8 (v4.0 8.7). Ignition 8.1.0 to 8.1.54 and 8.3.0 to 8.3.8 are affected, and 8.1.55 and 8.3.9 fix it. CISA reports no known public exploitation, the flaw is not in KEV, and the advisory lists the Critical Manufacturing, Energy and Information Technology sectors. It was one of two advisories CISA issued that day; the other covered a consumer Wi-Fi camera. The sector read is ours: Ignition is widely used for production monitoring, pipeline and gathering-system SCADA, terminal HMIs and the dashboards that pull data from all three, and privilege escalation on a SCADA gateway is how a stolen low-level login becomes more control than it should ever have had. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-286-01 (CSAF record as indexed by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup), corroborated by SecurityWeek; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Advisory published 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] A second critical lwIP flaw in two weeks: CISA flags a CVSS 9.8 buffer overflow in the SMTP client, after September’s MQTT client bug — exposure depends on each device vendor
item.category: Critical Advisory — Embedded TCP/IP stack; two critical client flaws in two weeks; exposure set by each device vendor
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-279-02 on 6 October for the SMTP client in lwIP 2.2.1, the lightweight open-source TCP/IP stack built into many controllers, gateways and sensors. CVE-2026-15340 is a classic buffer overflow that the advisory scores CVSS v3.1 9.8 (v4.0 9.3 in the CVE record). The fix is an upstream patch and commit rather than a new release, and CISA lists the Energy and Water and Wastewater sectors. It follows ICSA-26-265-01 of 22 September for lwIP’s MQTT client, CVE-2026-87121, an out-of-bounds write also scored 9.8 that may allow full code execution on the device; that batch also carried a second lwIP advisory, six Siemens republications and OpenPLC Runtime v3. Neither lwIP flaw is reported exploited or listed in KEV. Both sit in optional client applications inside a library, so whether a given RTU, flow computer, gas detector or wireless gateway is affected depends on whether its maker built in the SMTP or MQTT client — something only the device vendors can answer. Devices that email alarms or reports, or publish telemetry over MQTT, are the ones to ask about first. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-279-02 (6 Oct 2026) and ICSA-26-265-01 to -09 (22 Sep 2026), via CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup and CISA’s CSAF files; CVSS per the advisories and CVE records; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - MQTT client advisory 22 Sep 2026; SMTP client advisory 6 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] CISA: ten flaws, led by a CVSS 10.0 file-exposure bug, in Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT, terminal management software for midstream fuel terminals — fixed in 7.8, not exploited
item.category: Critical Advisory — Fuel and bulk-liquid terminal management software
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-272-02 on 29 September for Toptech Systems TMS7 and TopHAT version 7.6.3. It lists ten vulnerabilities. The most serious, CVE-2026-71379, leaves files or directories accessible to external parties and is scored CVSS v3.1 10.0 (v4 10.0). CVE-2026-70356 allows unrestricted upload of a dangerous file type (v3.1 9.1), and five SQL injection flaws — CVE-2026-72510, CVE-2026-63713, CVE-2026-68954, CVE-2026-68068 and CVE-2026-72507 — score v3.1 9.0. The rest are a session fixation flaw (v3.1 7.1) and two low-scoring eval-injection and cross-site scripting issues. CISA says successful exploitation could let an attacker access critical data or execute arbitrary code, lists the Energy, Chemical and Transportation Systems sectors, and says the products are deployed worldwide. The fix is release 7.8, which Toptech issued on 20 July with a customer advisory, so sites still on 7.6.3 have had a fix available for more than two months. No known public exploitation has been reported to CISA, and none of the flaws is in KEV. This one is squarely in the sector: Toptech, part of IDEX, describes itself as providing batch controller hardware and terminal management solutions for the midstream oil and gas industry, and TMS7 is part of its terminal management line. In a fuel or bulk-liquid terminal, software of this class typically authorises drivers and carriers, allocates product, produces bills of lading, keeps inventory and talks to the batch controllers at the loading rack (that description is ours, not CISA’s). A database or file-system compromise there is a commercial and operational problem even if no controller is touched. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-02 (CSAF record as indexed by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup); fix date per CISA; product and company description from Toptech’s website; the terminal-function description is editorial - Fix released 20 Jul 2026; CISA advisory published 29 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] An exploited FortiMail flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker write files on the mail gateway — in KEV since 1 October, and Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited email security gateway, CISA KEV
item.description: Fortinet published FG-IR-26-175 on 1 October for CVE-2026-104286, a path traversal flaw combined with improper NULL-byte handling in FortiMail. Fortinet says it lets an unauthenticated attacker “write arbitrary files on the underlying system via crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests”, scores it CVSS 9.8 and says it has been reported exploited in the wild; Fortinet found the flaw internally. CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 4 October federal deadline. Affected branches are 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1. When the advisory first appeared the fixed releases were listed as planned, with no date. Fortinet’s 5 October update now lists 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2 or later, and tells 7.2 users to move to the 7.4 branch or above. Its workarounds still matter until each unit is upgraded: disable Identity-Based Encryption (IBE), restrict webmail access from untrusted networks, and use web application firewall rules to block path-traversal requests to the IBE endpoint. No actor, campaign or victim has been disclosed. The sector read is ours: a mail gateway is not OT, but in oil and gas it is the relay for vendor advisories, nominations and scheduling, and the alarm and production-report email that leaves plant networks, and a file-write foothold on it is a trusted position next to the systems the business side of operations depends on. - Fortinet PSIRT advisory FG-IR-26-175 and its 5 Oct solution update; CISA KEV entry; launch-day fix status as reported by SecurityWeek; oil and gas relevance is editorial assessment - Advisory and KEV addition 1 Oct 2026 (due 4 Oct); fixed releases listed 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager: an exploited authentication bypass gives unauthenticated attackers admin-level API access to the system that configures every site — CVSS 9.8, in KEV since 30 September
item.category: Critical Advisory — Exploited SD-WAN management controller, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-76504 on 30 September. Improper handling of URI encoding in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager lets a remote, unauthenticated request get past an authentication rule meant to restrict a specific API endpoint, giving administrator-level access. Cisco scores it CVSS 9.8, says there are no workarounds, and states that its PSIRT “became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability” in September 2026. CISA added it to KEV on 30 September with a 3 October deadline, and Cisco revised the advisory to version 1.1 on 2 October. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1; releases older than 20.9 must migrate to a fixed release. BleepingComputer counts it as the fifth exploited Catalyst SD-WAN zero-day of 2026. No actor or victim has been named. The sector read is ours: where SD-WAN carries traffic between control centres, compressor and pump stations, terminals and field offices, the manager is the system that pushes configuration and policy to every edge router, so admin access to it is a route to changing segmentation at every site at once. It is the same exposure as the Arista VeloCloud orchestrator, where a third exploited flaw was patched on 22 October (see Arista VeloCloud). - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU (v1.1); CISA KEV entry; zero-day count per BleepingComputer; oil and gas WAN relevance is editorial assessment - Advisory and KEV addition 30 Sep 2026 (due 3 Oct); advisory revised 2 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] MikroTik RouterOS: the exploited “MikroTrick” chain is fully in KEV, and CISA now flags a separate pre-authentication CVSS 9.8 web-management flaw that is not — the routers at remote sites
item.category: Critical Advisory — Confirmed exploited, remote-site edge routers, CISA KEV
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-67279 in MikroTik RouterOS to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 25 September, with a federal remediation deadline of 28 September. It is an SSH workflow flaw that, in the KEV entry’s words, “could allow an unauthenticated client to open a session channel and send an exec request”, and that can be chained for unauthenticated exploitation of CVE-2026-86060; reporting gives it CVSS 6.9 without stating the version. It joins CVE-2026-86060, an argument-injection flaw, and CVE-2026-67277, a missing-authentication flaw in the bandwidth-test service, both added to KEV on 10 September. CERT Polska reported on 5 September that a two-flaw SSH chain it calls “MikroTrick” has been exploited in the wild since about 2 September. Its 22 September technical analysis names the chain: CVE-2026-67279 combined with CVE-2026-86060, which gives an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control. CVE-2026-67276, which an earlier edition of this card placed in the chain, is not in KEV. CERT Polska lists RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21 as fixed; a related flaw, CVE-2026-67278, needs 7.24.3 or 7.23.6 because the earlier fix was incomplete. Separately, CISA’s ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-06 of 29 September covers CVE-2026-84411, a pre-authentication integer underflow in RouterOS web management that can lead to code execution or denial of service, scored CVSS v3.1 9.8 and fixed in RouterOS 7.24 and later; no exploitation has been reported and it is not in KEV. Shadowserver counted more than 122,500 MikroTik devices with SSH reachable from the internet in early September — an exposure count, not a count of compromised or unpatched devices. No victims or sectors have been named, so there is no confirmed oil and gas victim. The sector read is ours: inexpensive, capable routers are a common contractor choice for cellular and fixed-wireless backhaul at wellpads, tank batteries, remote valve and meter stations and pipeline block-valve sites — often the one device on site with a route to both the SCADA host and the internet. - CISA KEV catalog entries of 10 and 25 Sep 2026; CERT Polska posts of 5 Sep 2026 and its 22 Sep 2026 technical analysis naming the chain; CVE-2026-67279 KEV addition and CVSS as reported by The Hacker News; Shadowserver exposure count as reported in early September. No victims or sectors named; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment; CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-06 for CVE-2026-84411 - Exploitation observed from about 2 Sep 2026; CERT Polska posts 5 Sep 2026; KEV additions 10 Sep 2026 and 25 Sep 2026 (due 28 Sep 2026); CISA ICS advisory for CVE-2026-84411 29 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Lantronix G520 cellular gateways do not properly verify software signatures — CISA says an attacker could replace the software and run code as root; fixed in 2.6.0.7R6
item.category: Critical Advisory — Cellular gateway for remote sites; software signature check
item.description: CISA published ICSA-26-272-01 on 29 September for the Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateway, version 2.6.0.4R6_stable. CVE-2026-91191 is an improper verification of a cryptographic signature and CVE-2026-84409 is a cross-site scripting flaw; each is scored CVSS v3.1 7.5 (v4 7.7). CISA says successful exploitation could allow an attacker to “replace software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges”. It lists the Energy, Water and Wastewater, and Transportation Systems sectors, with deployment worldwide. Lantronix release 2.6.0.7R6 fixes both. No known public exploitation has been reported to CISA, and neither flaw is in KEV. The sector read is ours: industrial cellular gateways like this are how many wellpads, tank batteries, meter stations and cathodic-protection sites get RTU and flow-computer data back to SCADA, and a gateway that will accept replaced software is a root foothold on the one device that bridges the site to the carrier network. It is the same remote-site edge question as the exploited MikroTik routers above, without the exploitation. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-01 (CSAF record as indexed by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup); oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Advisory published 29 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] One unauthenticated packet can crash TDengine, the time-series database some operators use behind telemetry and SCADA data — CVSS 7.5, fixed in 3.4.1.6, not exploited
item.category: Critical Advisory — Industrial time-series database, unauthenticated denial of service
item.description: Ridge Security disclosed CVE-2026-42542 on 23 September, a pre-authentication flaw in the RPC service of the open-source TDengine time-series database, which listens on TCP port 6030 by default. The vendor’s GitHub advisory, GHSA-vg95-j2hf-hvjx, describes an integer underflow in the uvConnMayGetUserInfo() function: a client-supplied message length is not validated, the calculation wraps around, and the resulting oversized memory copy crashes the taosd server process. No credentials or session are needed; a single crafted packet is enough. It is rated CVSS 7.5 (High), availability impact only. Affected are TDengine 3.4.0.0 through 3.4.1.5; the fix is 3.4.1.6. Ridge confirms remote denial of service, says plainly that it is not claiming code execution, and reports no telemetry of in-the-wild exploitation and no known public exploit code. Ridge names industrial telemetry, energy, utilities and factory-floor SCADA among the settings where TDengine runs. Its place on this page is editorial assessment: where a time-series store sits behind production, pipeline or compression telemetry, losing it blinds trending, alarm analytics and reporting even though control keeps running. - TDengine GitHub security advisory GHSA-vg95-j2hf-hvjx and Ridge Security disclosure, both reviewed directly; reported by Industrial Cyber (25 Sep 2026); oil and gas applicability is editorial assessment - Fix released with vendor advisory 4 Jun 2026; researcher disclosure 23 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] About 20 flaws in one shared IO-Link master firmware base hit three vendors at once — unauthenticated root at the field layer
item.category: Critical Advisory — Field-layer I/O, shared OEM firmware
item.description: CERT@VDE published three advisories on 16 September that carry the same CVE range, CVE-2026-27546 through CVE-2026-27565, across three different brands: VDE-2026-014 for Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-* and ICE3-* models, VDE-2026-027 for Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 EIP DI8 and IOL MA8 PN DI8, and VDE-2026-028 for Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 units. One shared CVE set across three vendors points to a common OEM firmware base. The worst two are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass at CVSS 9.8, and CVE-2026-27565, an OS command injection at CVSS 9.8 reachable over the network without authentication or user interaction; below them sit command-injection and local-file-inclusion flaws at 8.8, an authorisation bypass at 8.1, path traversal at 7.5 and information disclosure at 6.5. The outcome is unauthenticated root code execution on the device and theft of stored password hashes and SSH private keys. Firmware below 1.7.4 is affected and the advisories name 1.7.8 as fixed — confirm the exact build with your vendor. On 24 September Nozomi Networks Labs published its technical write-up of the Pepperl+Fuchs findings (VDE-2026-014), counting 19 CVEs on the ICE2-8IOL-K45P-RJ45 it tested and showing that, chained, they give an unauthenticated attacker root on the device and the ability to manipulate sensor and actuator data. No exploitation has been reported. IO-Link masters aggregate sensors and actuators onto EtherNet/IP and PROFINET segments; in oil and gas they usually arrive inside packaged equipment — metering and analyser cabinets, custody-transfer skids, vendor process packages — rather than in the main DCS I/O count, which is why they are easy to miss. - CERT@VDE advisories VDE-2026-014, VDE-2026-027 and VDE-2026-028; Nozomi Networks Labs technical write-up of VDE-2026-014; oil and gas deployment context is editorial assessment - Advisories published 16 Sep 2026; Nozomi write-up 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] Coast Guard NVIC 02-26 sets out how vessels, port facilities and Outer Continental Shelf facilities should build the cyber plans due by 16 July 2027 — penetration testing is not required for the first plan
item.category: Guidance — Coast Guard implementation guidance for the maritime cyber rule; covers Outer Continental Shelf facilities; plans due 16 Jul 2027
item.description: The US Coast Guard has issued Navigation and Vessel Inspection Circular 02-26, its guidance on meeting the cybersecurity requirements of 33 CFR Part 101 Subpart F, the maritime cyber rule. Industrial Cyber reported it on 23 October; the Coast Guard’s file name dates it 19 October. It applies to US-flagged vessels, MTSA-regulated facilities and Outer Continental Shelf facilities, and walks through designating a qualified Cybersecurity Officer, carrying out the Cybersecurity Assessment and writing the Cybersecurity Plan, including identifying critical IT and OT systems and how they depend on each other. All three are due to the Coast Guard by 16 July 2027. Penetration testing is not required for the first plan; an enclosure sets out expectations, including OT safety, for the five-year renewal cycle, and another offers an optional method based on the NIST Cybersecurity Framework for scoping critical systems. The approach is performance-based: the Coast Guard does not prescribe products or require third-party assessors. An NVIC explains how to comply; it does not change the rule’s deadlines. The fit for this page is direct for offshore facilities on the Outer Continental Shelf and, in our reading, for the marine oil, fuel and LNG terminals that are MTSA-regulated facilities (editorial assessment). - US Coast Guard NVIC 02-26 as reported by Industrial Cyber (23 Oct 2026); issue date inferred from the Coast Guard file name; the circular itself was not retrieved; oil and gas terminal fit is editorial assessment - Dated 19 Oct 2026 (per file name); reported 23 Oct 2026; plans due 16 Jul 2027

item.title: [Info] Accenture, Dragos and SANS launch a foundation offering free OT monitoring, deployment and training to up to 500 small utilities — natural gas utilities are eligible, and enrolment opens soon
item.category: Programme — Free OT monitoring, deployment and training for small utilities, natural gas included; private funding, no new requirement
item.description: On 20 October Accenture, Dragos and the SANS Institute launched the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation, a nonprofit with about US$10 million in initial funding and services, with Elastic providing technology support. Its first phase covers up to 500 utilities with annual revenue under US$100 million, on top of the more than 100 already in Dragos’s Community Defense Program. Participants get Dragos Platform access, Neighborhood Keeper and Dragos’s OT-CERT; assessment, deployment, configuration and ongoing support from Accenture; SANS OnDemand training with GIAC certification; and hardware funding where needed. The foundation’s site lists electric, natural gas, water and wastewater utilities in the US and Canada, while Dragos’s announcement speaks of US utilities; enrolment “opens soon”, with an interest list in the meantime. There is no government involvement. “Access was never the problem. Knowing help was available and adoption was,” Dragos’s Robert M. Lee wrote. For this sector the fit is municipal and small investor-owned gas distribution systems, which run SCADA, gate, regulator and odorisation stations with few security staff (editorial assessment). - Dragos announcement (20 Oct 2026) and the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation website; government involvement per The Record (21 Oct 2026); natural gas fit is editorial assessment - Announced 20 Oct 2026; enrolment not yet open

item.title: [Info] The OT Cybersecurity Coalition presses CISA again for a binding directive on federal agencies’ own OT, now citing the French refrigeration attack — a proposal, not a CISA action
item.category: Policy — Industry proposal for a federal OT directive, renewed after the French attack; no CISA action
item.description: CyberScoop reported on 6 October that the OT Cybersecurity Coalition has published a paper urging CISA to issue a Binding Operational Directive focused solely on operational technology at federal civilian agencies. The coalition wants the directive to assign responsibility at each agency, including an accountable OT cybersecurity officer, set minimum practices drawn from existing federal guidance, align with CISA’s 2022 Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, and consider whether NSA’s OT guidance should apply to civilian agencies. In its words, “it is time for an encompassing BOD solely focused on OT security.” Earlier directives touched OT without being built for it. CISA did not respond to CyberScoop and has announced no directive. The paper leans on GAO-26-108937, published on 30 September: of 22 civilian CFO Act agencies reviewed, 15 had established inventories of networked IoT and OT devices, 11 maintained them, 10 included all required information, and only 7 met all three OMB requirements. GAO’s one recommendation is that OMB issue updated guidance covering these devices and oversee implementation. A directive would bind federal agencies only; the coalition’s argument is that it would also signal to the private sector what the government expects. On 14 October the coalition returned to the subject after the French supermarket refrigeration attack: in a statement reported by Industrial Cyber, it said failures in cybersecurity fundamentals had led to a significant incident, repeated ANSSI’s advice on VPN-only remote access, default passwords and firmware, renewed its call for a binding OT directive, and warned that refrigeration controllers could become an attack vector in the United States too, while noting that no US incidents have been reported. For oil and gas operators the practical value today is GAO’s three tests, which work as a self-check on your own OT asset inventory. - OT Cybersecurity Coalition paper as reported by CyberScoop (6 Oct 2026); coalition statement of 14 Oct 2026 as reported by Industrial Cyber (16 Oct 2026); GAO-26-108937; no CISA directive found as of 16 Oct 2026 - GAO report published 30 Sep 2026; coalition proposal reported 6 Oct 2026; follow-up statement 14 Oct 2026
