item.title: [Info] GAO: industry panelists, energy among them, say overlapping federal cyber rules are hard to satisfy while fighting an incident — and the CIRCIA final rule is now under White House review
item.category: Policy — Federal incident reporting; GAO report, no new requirement
item.description: The Government Accountability Office published GAO-26-109197, “Cybersecurity Regulations: Industry Panelists Identify Duplication and Conflicts and Ways to Address Them”, on 28 September. It records a virtual panel held on 16 July with six industry representatives from the energy, financial services, and healthcare and public health sectors. Panelists said it could be difficult to meet every reporting requirement while also remediating a cyber threat, saw DHS and SEC rules as duplicating sector-specific ones, and half of them agreed that progress on harmonisation has been limited. Their suggestions were consistent timeframes, thresholds and definitions; a lead agency, such as CISA, to coordinate reporting; and more collaboration between government and industry. Cybersecurity Dive reports that energy participants named TSA pipeline reporting and NERC CIP among the overlapping regimes. The report makes no formal GAO recommendations. It adds to a count already in circulation: on 8 September the McCrary Institute and the US Chamber of Commerce, drawing on GAO work, tallied 117 federal cyber incident reporting regulations across 27 agencies, 48 of which apply to private industry. The rule most likely to change the picture has not arrived. CISA has now sent its CIRCIA final rule to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, which logged it for review on 1 October; the text is not public, the statutory deadline passed a year ago, and HIPAA Journal reports publication is expected before year-end. Once in force, covered incidents are to be reported within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24, from dates the final rule sets. Oil and gas operators will recognise the problem: one event can trigger TSA pipeline security directive reporting to CISA, Coast Guard reporting for regulated terminals, SEC disclosure, state regulators, insurers and contractual notices. - GAO-26-109197, with coverage by Cybersecurity Dive and Industrial Cyber; McCrary Institute and US Chamber of Commerce analysis as reported by Industrial Cyber; CIRCIA status from the reginfo.gov regulatory review record and HIPAA Journal - McCrary analysis 8 Sep 2026; GAO report published 28 Sep 2026; CIRCIA final rule received for OIRA review 1 Oct 2026, not yet published

item.title: [Info] CISA’s “Securing the Next 250” campaign: reduce attack surfaces, replace end-of-support devices, recover quickly — voluntary, but the end-of-support message lands on the field edge
item.category: Policy — CISA awareness campaign; voluntary, no new requirement
item.description: CISA has launched “Securing the Next 250” for Cybersecurity Awareness Month, as reported by Industrial Cyber on 2 October. It is built around three Rs: Reduce attack surfaces, Replace end-of-support devices, and Recover quickly to sustain operations. Acting Director Nick Andersen framed it around dependency: when critical infrastructure is disrupted, “so are the businesses and communities that depend on vital services.” Beyond the three Rs the campaign promotes logging, backing up and encrypting data, reporting incidents to CISA, and keeping an incident response plan that is exercised, with realistic drills that include leadership and legal counsel at least once a year, and it singles out replacing end-of-support edge devices. It is guidance and promotion, not a requirement. The fit for oil and gas is editorial but direct: this edition’s exploited edge flaws — MikroTik routers, Citrix and Ivanti gateways, Cisco SD-WAN and FortiMail — are the class of device the Replace message is aimed at, and remote sites are where routers, gateways and switches tend to outlive their vendor support. - CISA campaign as reported by Industrial Cyber; oil and gas framing is editorial - Reported 2 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] Texas Railroad Commissioner Wayne Christian cites the tanker boardings and urges operators to “invest, test, monitor and strengthen” cyber defences — a statement, not a new rule
item.category: Policy — State oil and gas regulator statement; no incident reported; no new requirement
item.description: On 24 September the Railroad Commission of Texas issued a press release quoting Commissioner Wayne Christian, urging the state’s energy industry to prepare for evolving cyber threats. It is a commissioner’s statement, not a formal advisory or notice to operators, and it sets no new requirement and gives no technical guidance. It cites the August Coast Guard and FBI boarding of two foreign-flagged energy vessels bound for US ports, naming VL Prosperity, the crude tanker bound for Galveston (see the top story), and separate federal warnings that China-linked and Iran-affiliated cyber actors are targeting US critical infrastructure, including internet-connected operational technology and industrial control systems. It says it follows a notice the Commission sent to regulated operators earlier this year. Christian is quoted: “Texas is the energy capital of the world, and that makes our energy infrastructure a prime target for foreign adversaries,” and “We must invest, test, monitor and strengthen our defenses now.” He also calls for using AI to defend critical infrastructure. The statement reports no incident at any Texas operator and does not mention the Vivit Africa LNG carrier. For Texas producers, pipelines, processors and terminals, the practical read is that the state’s oil and gas regulator is publicly linking the maritime cargo compromises to operator readiness. - Railroad Commission of Texas press release quoting Commissioner Wayne Christian, as distributed via EIN Presswire and reported by World Oil; no incident reported - Issued 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA and FBI put a number on integrator risk: one compromised automation vendor, nine archives, roughly 800 files of customers’ SCADA information and schematics
item.category: Guidance — CISA and FBI joint fact sheet on third-party ICS integrator risk; no CVE
item.description: CISA and the FBI released a joint fact sheet, dated 23 September and publicised on 24 September, “Considerations for Critical Infrastructure Operators Working With Third-Party ICS Integrators”. It is built on a case from March and April 2025, when foreign cyber actors compromised the network of a US industrial automation company that provided system integration, engineering consulting and SCADA programming to industrial customers, including power utilities and transportation entities. Once inside, the actors searched for terms including “customers” and “SCADA” and staged roughly 800 files — customer SCADA information, ICS device details and schematics — in nine compressed archives for exfiltration. The fact sheet does not name the integrator, its customers or the actor, and describes no disruption. Its core advice is to limit every integrator connection to what a task requires and to replace continuous vendor connections with on-demand remote access that the operator enables, monitors and disables. No oil and gas customer is named; the relevance here is editorial assessment, because pipeline SCADA, compressor-station, wellsite-automation and terminal projects are routinely built and maintained by the same kind of integrator. - CISA and FBI joint fact sheet (dated 23 Sep 2026, publicised 24 Sep 2026), case details as re-posted TLP:CLEAR by WaterISAC and reviewed directly; also reported by Industrial Cyber and SecurityWeek; oil and gas applicability is editorial assessment - Dated 23 Sep 2026; publicised 24 Sep 2026
